newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Energis sees alliance in 12 months.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Energis sees alliance in 12 months.

text.p: Energis, the UK telecommunications service strung beneath the National Grid's high voltage electricity pylons, said on Monday it was on track to announcing a link with an international carrier within the next 12 months.

Energis' chief executive Mike Grabiner told Reuters that the company, which is wholly owned by the National Grid, needed an international company to help boost its service but declined to divulge with whom the company was talking.
"From our point of view, we have national capability and we need to take an international partner to help us develop our international business," he said.
"We're still on track to do that (announce an alliance) within the next 12 months," he added.

Grabiner, speaking after the company unveiled what it called record low business rates to the U.S. of 10 pence a minute, said the group was investing in its own capacity and switches so it could be independent when it won an international licence.

The Department of Trade and Industry is expected to award a number of international licences at the end of November, ending the British Telecommunications and Mercury duopoly on the operation of international lines out of the UK. Grabiner said about 40 telecom companies had applied for a licence.
At the moment, Energis has to rent line capacity from BT and Cable & Wireless' Mercury to get calls out of the UK.

Without an international licence, it also has to negotiate rates individually with international operators such as Sweden's Telia AB, Australia's Telstra Corp, Sprint Corp and Teleglobe Inc from Canada.
BT and Mercury, on the other hand, can get access to international capacity at cost rates.

Energis said its new U.S. business rate undercut BT's base rate by 50 percent and BT's best rate by 40 percent. The group also boasts a minimum differential of 24 percent below BT's base rate on daytime calls to Australasia, Japan and the Far East.
In the UK, busines rates are 42 percent below BT's base rates and undercut its discounted rates by 10 percent, it said.
"We can sustain these rates," Grabiner said. "But until we get an international licence, BT and Mercury's cost structure is a lot lower than ours."
The company, which serves about 12,000 customers, made an operating loss of 72.8 million stg last year. It still expects to break even in 1999/2000.
